segments.titre: China's marriage crisis as a financial auction
segments.resume: The video opens by claiming China is collapsing behind its superpower image, with a demographic crisis driven by money rather than a cultural turn against marriage. Courtship is described as a ruthless financial auction in which young men are priced out of dating and forced to liquidate family savings.
segments.texte: China is collapsing. While projecting superpower strength on the global stage, the reality at home is much different. A demographic crisis is brewing. Mainstream narratives claim that people are turning their backs on marriage to chase modern single lifestyles. It’s all a lie. In today’s China, courtship is no longer about romance or relationships. It’s a ruthless financial auction. Young men are being priced out of dates, forced to liquidate generations of savings just to meet someone. This isn’t a cultural shift. Beneath the opulent banquet halls and desperate match making market, there’s a sinister, darker reality… And it’s about to threaten the entire economy.

segments.titre: Empty banquet halls and record-low marriages
segments.resume: Wedding venues that once needed months of advance booking now sit empty across China, hurting a country that needs births. Registered marriages fell from 13.47 million in 2013 to 6.11 million in 2024, and the first half of 2026 recorded 3.275 million, the lowest half-year since 1980.
segments.texte: A decade ago, a couple waiting to get married would have needed to book a popular wedding venue months in advance. Today, thousands of banquet halls across China are lying empty. Fewer and fewer people are getting married. And in a country struggling to increase its birth rate to avoid a total demographic collapse, the death of the wedding market is a disaster. The numbers are brutal. In 2013, China registered 13.47 million marriages, the highest on record. By 2024, that had fallen to 6.11 million. More than half. Gone in just over a decade. And the trend is accelerating. The first six months of 2026 saw t 3.275 million marriages, down another 7.5% year-on-year. It’s the lowest half-year total that China has recorded since it began keeping nationwide records in 1980.

segments.titre: Weddings as a transaction with a hefty entrance fee
segments.resume: Men are weighing the financial implications of marriage rather than failing to show up at the altar. The wedding has become a transaction whose entry fee has risen for two decades and now equals years of a family's income, leaving tens of millions of men at risk of never marrying.
segments.texte: The men at the center of this destructive spiral aren’t standing at the altar, wondering why the bride hasn’t shown up. They’re standing outside, weighing up the financial implications. Because in large parts of China, a wedding is no longer a ceremony. It’s a transaction. And it comes with a hefty entrance fee. That fee has been rising steadily for 2 decades, and is now measured in years of a family’s income. The result is tens of millions of men who face a risk of never marrying.

segments.titre: Excess males and the shortage of brides
segments.resume: Demographers estimate about 30 million excess men aged 20 to 45, a figure projected to reach 41 million by the early 2040s, and the 2020 census counted 17.52 million more men than women aged 20 to 40. The one-child policy and son preference discouraged female births, and the shortage hits poor rural provinces like Jiangxi and Gansu hardest.
segments.texte: Demographers estimate that there are around 30 million excess males aged between 20 and 45 in China. It’s the product of decades of more boys being born than girls. Some projections estimate that the peak hasn’t been hit yet. The number is expected to hit 41 million by the early 2040s. The 2020 census counted 17.52 million more men than women in the prime 20 to 40 age bracket. But whatever the number is today, the scale is enormous. And the problem is escalating. For more than 3 decades, China’s famous one-child policy, combined with a deep cultural preference for sons, discouraged the births of girls. The result can be seen on the streets today. There are fewer women. To make matters worse, the shortage of potential brides isn’t evenly distributed. It hits hardest in the poorer provinces, and punishes the men with the least to offer a prospective family. In the richest cities, a shortage of women exists on paper. But in a rural county in Jiangxi or Gansu, you can see it with your eyes on the street.

segments.titre: Caili: the bride price and its explosion
segments.resume: Caili is the betrothal payment from the groom's family to the bride's family, present in almost three quarters of Chinese marriages. Wuhan University research found rural bride prices rose from 10,000-20,000 yuan in the early 2000s to 140,000 yuan by 2021.
segments.texte: Getting married in China doesn’t work the same way as in the West. Central to the Chinese marriage process is a custom called caili. It’s a betrothal payment made by the groom’s family to the bride’s. It’s been at the heart of Chinese marriage for centuries. Essentially, men have to bid for a bride. Today, it appears in almost three quarters of Chinese marriages. The custom itself hasn’t changed much over the years. But the size of the bids has. Research from Wuhan University revealed that rural bride prices in the early 2000s were around 10,000 to 20,000 yuan, around $1,500 to $3,000. By 2021, they had exploded to 140,000 yuan, or $21,000. A payment that once cost a family a few months to save now takes several years. And it varies from region to region.

segments.titre: Regional bride prices and years of income
segments.resume: Average bride prices reach 130,000 yuan in Jiangxi and over 180,000 yuan in Zhejiang, with demands up to 2 million yuan in parts of Fujian, before the apartment and car. Against rural disposable income of about 24,400 yuan, a 380,000-yuan price equals roughly 6 years of household income, or 15 for a single man.
segments.texte: The Jiangxi Women’s Federation put its own province’s average at 130,000 yuan, or $19,000 in early 2023. In Zhejiang, one of the wealthiest provinces, it’s over 180,000 yuan, about $27,000. And that’s the average. In parts of Fujian, families can demand up to 2 million yuan, or $300,000. That’s just the bride price. Grooms still have to pay for an apartment and car, which are usually a separate conversation. There are two reasons why these numbers are so hard for so many men and their families to handle. China’s rural per-capita disposable income was about 24,400 yuan, or $3,700 a year in 2025. So a 380,000-yuan bride price is roughly 6 years of disposable income for a rural household of that size. For a single man saving by himself, it’s closer to 15 years. The other reason is that the market is skewed.

segments.titre: Poorest men pay the highest bride prices
segments.resume: Research in the Chinese Journal of Sociology found that poorer grooms can face higher bride prices, while wealthier families with status are quoted less. A matchmaker's remark shows the logic: the price is a guarantee the bride's family keeps its money.
segments.texte: You’d think that poorer prospective grooms would get a break. They don’t. Research published in the Chinese Journal of Sociology found that bride prices can be higher for poorest men. Wealthier families with status get quoted less. As one matchmaker bluntly put it, “Even if you do not care for my daughter someday, you will at least cherish your money.”

segments.titre: Bride-price disputes and the Supreme People's Court law
segments.resume: Over 140,000 bride-price disputes fill China's court database, with prices typically 3 to 10 times the groom's annual disposable income. Prices are kept by the bride's parents in the south and passed to the bride in the north, and the Supreme People's Court rule only governs failed deals without lowering prices.
segments.texte: Behind this ruthless logic, there’s a legal system playing catch up. More than 140,000 bride-price disputes clog China’s court judgments database. A 2022 study of those cases found that bride prices typically ran between 3 and 10 times the groom’s annual disposable income. Almost 69% of the disputes involved sums between 50,000 and 150,000 yuan, about $7,500 to $22,000. But this isn’t just about culture. There’s a calculated strategy involved. In the south of the country, the payment is usually kept by the bride’s parents, and described as child-rearing money. But in the north, it’s usually passed to the bride, which gives northern families less room to bargain. The crisis has gotten so bad that the Supreme People’s Court stepped in, passing a law to stop families from using weddings to extort money. But that law completely misses the point. It only governs what happens when the deal fails. It does nothing to lower the price. The net result is as mercenary as it gets. Families pay, or they don’t marry.

segments.titre: Marriage markets in Shanghai and Beijing parks
segments.resume: Parents set up umbrellas with ads for their children at People's Park in Shanghai, a market running since about 2004 and organized by birth decade. An analysis of 874 ads found looks, job and property dominate, with personality in 38% and hobbies in 11%, and Beijing parents ask where the house is.
segments.texte: It’s devastating for families, and it doesn’t need statistics to prove it. On weekends in Shanghai, parents go to People’s Park and set up umbrellas. Clipped to those umbrellas are advertisements. Not for products, but for their children. This human trading floor has been running since around 2004. It's divided into zones sorted by the decade the child was born. Sixth Tone and The Paper analyzed 874 of those ads. The priorities are obvious: looks, job, and property ownership. Personality appeared in 38% of them. Hobbies in just 11%. In Beijing, at Zhongshan Park, the requirements are even more ruthless. Housing there isn’t a yes-or-no question. The parents demand to know “Where is your house?” To get married in modern China, you need a massive cash dowry and prime real estate in the country’s most expensive neighborhoods. It’s not the only requirement.

segments.titre: The Beijing blind-date price list
segments.resume: A viral Beijing blind-date price list sorts people into financial tiers down to a 'no consideration' category, and matchmaking events are designed for haggling. The top male tier required 5.6 million yuan net worth, a home in a central district and 50,000 yuan monthly income, versus 20,000 yuan and a degree for women.
segments.texte: A Beijing blind-date price list went viral and it revealed a dystopian system that sorts humans into financial tier. The rankings range from top class down to a category harshly labeled “no consideration”. Blind-date matchmaking events are a feature of the Chinese marriage industry but they’re not just designed to help find the one. They’re designed to haggle. For a man to reach the top tier, the list required a net worth of at least 5.6 million yuan, around $834,000, own home in one of Beijing’s 3 central districts, and earn more than 50,000 yuan, or $7,500, a month. For a woman, the top tier required an income above 20,000 yuan, roughly $3,000, a university degree and the same elite housing requirements. It’s not romance.

segments.titre: Rejection at matchmaking markets and dismal success rates
segments.resume: A 30-year-old Hong Kong blogger was rejected at Guangzhou's Tianhe Park in December 2024 over her height. A 2012 study found only 3 of 65 cases at the Shanghai market ended in a match, yet parents keep returning to avoid a son staying single.
segments.texte: It's filtering out the unwanted. In December 2024, a Hong Kong fashion blogger took a 3-hour train to Guangzhou’s Tianhe Park to try her luck among the umbrellas. She was instantly rejected. She was 30 years old, and stood 5’1” (1.54 cm). An inch and a half under the national average. One matchmaking mother turned her away saying the blogger’s height would affect her chance of having children. With standards set so high and prices to match, the success rates of these matchmaking markets are dismal. A 2012 study documented 65 cases at the Shanghai market. 3 of them ended in a match. But the parents keep coming back. The alternative is a son stays single forever.

segments.titre: Housing as the real obstacle to marriage
segments.resume: Housing makes up about 59% of Chinese household assets according to the central bank in 2019, and urban homeownership is 96% versus 65% in the US. Requiring an apartment means the groom's family must liquidate its savings into one asset, and location, such as inside Beijing's Third Ring Road, matters hugely.
segments.texte: But it’s not just the eyewatering dowry that is crippling single men. The housing situation is the real killer. In China, housing is the single most important asset most families hold, and sometimes the only one. In 2019, China’s central bank found that housing accounted for about 59% of all household assets. Nearly 70% of everything a typical Chinese family owns is tied up in the roof over their head. Financial assets come to about 20%. Cars, business assets and durables make up most of the rest. Because of this, urban homeownership sits at a staggering 96%. For comparison, American homeownership runs at 65%. So when a bride’s family insists on a potential groom having an apartment, they are not asking for a luxury. They are demanding the groom’s family liquidate everything they have ever saved, pour it into a single asset and hand over a share. That’s why the location matters so much. An apartment inside Beijing’s Third Ring Road is a different financial instrument from one in a distant suburb. Every single family in the market knows it.

segments.titre: Wedding costs versus the apartment and the property slump
segments.resume: The average 2021 wedding cost 174,000 yuan, about 9 months of couple income, but an apartment brings 30 years of mortgage, so it is the asset the market cares about. A man's marriageability now depends on his parents' single property, while by late 2026 more than half of home sales are second-hand and prices fall.
segments.texte: It’s caused a fundamental shift in how the marriage market functions. Historically, the wedding used to be the most expensive part. In 2021, the average Chinese wedding cost 174,000 yuan, around $26,000. That’s nearly 9 times a couple’s average monthly income. Meanwhile, 42% of couples went over budget. But a wedding lasts one day. An apartment has 30 years of mortgage payments. That’s why it’s the only asset the market actually cares about. And it’s created a bizarre, doomed incentive system. A man’s marriageability now depends on his parents’ balance sheet. And his parents’ balance sheet is almost entirely one property. That’s a problem. Because the Chinese property market has spent decades heading in one direction. Down. The crisis is so severe, that by late 2026, more than half of home sales across China were second-hand properties. Families have their savings tied up in older apartments and desperate buyers have the leverage to negotiate them down. So, when a family commits three generations of savings to a single apartment, they’re placing the entire family’s future on one bet.

segments.titre: Beijing's half-hearted response to bride prices
segments.resume: No Chinese law caps bride prices; the government relies on guidance, pilots and voluntary pledges without penalties. Wedding customs appeared in the No. 1 central document 7 times in 8 years, and 8 central departments ran a 2022 campaign, yet nothing changed.
segments.texte: And their son’s future is the collateral. You’d think the government would step in and stop this implosion. But Beijing’s response has been minimal. Any attempts to fix it have been half hearted. There’s no Chinese law that caps bride prices. Instead, the government relies on guidance, pilot programs and voluntary pledges that carry no financial penalties. They’ve been trying to stop the rot for years. Every single February, China releases its No. 1 central document, the most important policy paper of the year that sets rural priorities. Wedding customs have now appeared in it 7 times in the last 8 years. 8 different central departments launched a campaign to suppress bride prices in 2022. The Supreme People’s Court has weighed in repeatedly. Yet nothing changes. It’s so bad the state tried to micro-manage weddings right down to the local level. It illustrates the size of the problem and how difficult it is to rein in.

segments.titre: Local caps and pilot programs
segments.resume: Gansu capped bride prices at 50,000 yuan and banquets at 20 tables, a Shandong village rewrote its rules to 20,000-30,000 yuan, and Shicheng County set a symbolic price with incentives like loans and free pregnancy checks.
segments.texte: In Gansu province, officials set a cap of 50,000 yuan, about $7,300, on bride prices and limited banquets to 20 tables. A village in Shandong went as far as rewriting its village rules. It pushed bride prices down to between 20,000 and 30,000 yuan, equivalent to $3,000 to $4,500. . And in Shicheng County, the government pilot program set a symbolic bride price of a few thousand yuan. They even handed out incentives that unlocked loans, tourist-site entry and free pregnancy checks just to reward couples who didn’t price gouge each other.

segments.titre: Why the official results are weak
segments.resume: Official data shows families paying under 50,000 yuan rose from 16% to over 27%, meaning nearly 3 in 4 still pay market rates. A Jiangxi official admitted prices of 188,000 and 288,000 yuan are normal, showing the state cannot control its marriage market because compliance means becoming poorer.
segments.texte: On paper, it looks like the government is making a change. Official data shows that the share of families paying less than 50,000 yuan rose from 16% to over 27%. It sounds impressive. The reality isn’t. If 27 percent of families paid under the cap, it means that almost 3 out of 4 still paid the illegal market rate. They are completely ignoring the state’s warnings in villages that are supposed to follow the rules. A city official in Jiangxi admitted that prices of 188,000 and 288,000 yuan - around $28,000 and $43,000 - are normal in poorer areas. They said it would be unrealistic and to stop the custom. The authoritarian state is admitting it can’t control its own marriage market. And the reason is simple. Asking a family to ignore the going rate in the name of civic duty isn’t a noble act. It is asking them to become poorer.

segments.titre: A negotiation refunded at the Party office
segments.resume: In one case a man asked local government to regulate bride prices, and officials found his girlfriend's parents asked about 270,000 yuan. The father settled around 60,000 yuan and returned the rest at the local Communist Party office with officials watching.
segments.texte: In one case, a man asked his local government to regulate bride prices. Officials visited his girlfriend’s home and found that parents had been asking about 270,000 yuan, about $40,000. The father eventually settled at around 60,000 yuan. That’s $9,000. He returned the rest. The refund took place at the local Communist Party office, with party officials watching on. But cases like these are the exception rather than the rule.

segments.titre: A financial problem set by the market, not the state
segments.resume: The state can influence one negotiation but not a million, because prices are set by the market with far more players than the state has officials. The marriage crisis is financial rather than social, leaving tens of millions of men without a realistic chance of marrying while banquet halls gather dust.
segments.texte: The state can influence one negotiation. It hasn't found a way to influence a million of them. That’s because prices aren’t set by the government. They’re set by the market. And the market has many more players in it than the state has officials. The marriage crisis in China isn’t due to social changes. It’s financial. Grooms are being squeezed by mercenary families. Now, tens of millions of men are left without a realistic chance of getting married. The housing market is collapsing. And the banquet halls are

segments.titre: Ripple effects on jewelry, photography and hotels
segments.resume: In the first half of 2026 jewelry sales fell by about a third, nearly 2,000 chain stores closed, and diamond trade shrank by $6.4 billion, with soaring gold prices masking the decline. Bojue suspended its wedding photo division in July 2025, and 5-star hotels set up street food stalls to recoup wedding losses.
segments.texte: gathering dust. And the effects ripple out across the whole economy. In the first half of 2026, jewelry sales in China fell by about a third. National chains saw nearly 2,000 stores shuttered. Even though the industry giants are masking this decline with soaring gold prices, which artificially inflate their profits, actual sales have plummeted. The diamond trade saw its market shrink by $6.4 billion dollars. From jewellery to photography, businesses are disappearing overnight. Bojue, the company that built China’s destination wedding-photo industry, suspended its wedding division in July 2025. Customers and staff were left stranded. 5 star hotels across China have started setting up street food stalls outside their own entrances, selling crayfish and roast duck to passers-by just to recoup the losses from the dying wedding market. And no weddings means no children.

segments.titre: Falling births, kindergarten closures and rising cost per child
segments.resume: China closed over 21,000 kindergartens, preschool enrollment fell about 10%, and a Shanghai obstetrician warned his specialty was close to collapse. Births in 2025 hit 7.92 million, the lowest since 1949, while families concentrate wealth so cost per child reaches 72,000 yuan by 2030.
segments.texte: China closed over 21,000 kindergartens. Preschool enrollment fell about 10%. In 2026, a Shanghai obstetrician urged the country to save his specialty, warning it was on the verge of collapse.. Births in 2025 fell to 7.92 million, the lowest since 1949. But this demographic collapse has a bizarre economic twist. Fewer babies do not mean less spending. Families are concentrating their wealth, driving the cost per child up to 72,000 yuan, $10,700, by 2030. The maternity market is shrinking, but the money is going somewhere.

segments.titre: The single economy
segments.resume: Spending flows into a single economy worth over a trillion dollars a year, as a quarter of Chinese households have one person. It includes karaoke booths, hired hiking companions and photographers, games, streaming, AI companions, micro-dramas and the viral 'Are You Dead?' check-in app.
segments.texte: And where it goes tells you more about modern China than any of the collapse statistics. It fueled the rise of the single economy, a market worth more than a trillion U.S. dollars a year. With a quarter of all Chinese households now consisting of 1 person, a new ecosystem has emerged. The spending isn’t lonely in the traditional sense. Millions of dollars are flowing into miniature karaoke booths, booked by the hour. Hired hiking companions, sightseeing partners, and personal photographers. Video games, streaming subscriptions, AI companions and micro-dramas with episodes under 2 minutes. The shift is so intense that a viral app launched to check in on people living alone is literally called “Are You Dead?” An entire economy has been built on being single.

segments.titre: Men locked out of love and the economy
segments.resume: Unmarried men face 18.9% youth unemployment for ages 16-24, a figure the government changed by removing students from the methodology. A man in a poor province faces a multi-year bride price, an apartment requirement and a graduate-saturated job market, so men are unable to bid rather than refusing marriage.
segments.texte: So where does that leave the men hoping for a bride? Well, they’re locked out of love. And they’re locked out of the economy. China’s youth unemployment rate for 16- to 24-year-olds has surged to 18.9%. It's a number so worrying, the government removed students from the methodology to manipulate the number. A man in a poorer province faces a bride price that is equivalent to several years of his family’s income. He’s looking at an apartment requirement that swallows whatever is left. And an entry-level job market where he has to compete with millions of graduates for work that may not pay enough to seem like an attractive option. Men aren’t refusing to marry.

segments.titre: The demographic cliff and the failed marriage rebound
segments.resume: China faces births at their lowest since 1949 and deaths at their highest since 1968. Marriages rose 10.8% to 6.76 million in 2025 after registration rules changed in May 2025 and local cash incentives, but fell 6.24% in Q1 2026 and hit a record low in H1 2026.
segments.texte: They’re unable to bid. Now, the country is standing at the edge of a demographic cliff. Births at their lowest since 1949.. Deaths at their highest since 1968. But there is one glimmer of hope. In 2025, marriages rose 10.8% to 6.76 million, the first real increase in years. Officials had changed the rules in May 2025 so couples could register wherever they lived. Some local authorities paid newlyweds cash incentives to sweeten the deal. For a moment, it looked like China had turned the corner. Then it all came crashing down again. The first quarter of 2026 saw marriages fall by 6.24%. And it got worse. The first 6 months of the year set a new record low. And now China has more empty banquet halls that it used to easily fill. The state capped the daughters. The market priced out the sons. And an entire generation walked away from the future the state forced on them.

segments.titre: Outro: Japan's demographic collapse
segments.resume: The video notes the problem extends beyond China and points to Japan's own demographic collapse. It recommends another video on Japan's 2.8 million shut-ins and the hikikomori crisis.
segments.texte: This isn’t a problem that’s just confined to China’s borders. Japan is also looking at its own demographic collapse. Watch “Japan Is Dead. The 2.8 Million Shut Ins Tell The REAL Story.” to see how the growing hikikomori crisis is out of control. Or click on this.
